# Equal Temperament

The piano had not been played in eleven years, and Ines could tell before she lifted the lid. There is a particular silence that settles into an unplayed instrument, a dust not of the surface but of the wood itself. She pressed middle C and the note came out tired, a half-step lower than it had any right to be, like a man answering the door in his bathrobe at noon.

"It's bad," said Mr. Adair. It was not a question.

"It's asleep," she said. "Bad is different."

He was perhaps eighty, thin in the way of men who had once been broad, and he stood in the doorway of his own living room as if he needed permission to enter it. The room was clean. Someone dusted. But the chairs were arranged to face the television, and the piano sat against the far wall like a guest nobody had introduced.

"My wife played," he said. "I don't."

Ines nodded and opened her case. She had heard this sentence, in one form or another, perhaps two hundred times. *My daughter played. My mother played. We bought it for the grandchildren.* Pianos outlived their reasons. They were too heavy to move and too expensive to throw away, so they stayed, accumulating photographs on their tops like barnacles.

This one had no photographs. That was unusual.

She removed the fallboard and the music desk and looked in at the strings, the long bronze-wound basses and the bright steel trebles, the hammers lined up in their felt like a choir waiting for a downbeat. She set her tuning hammer on the first pin and began.

Mr. Adair did not leave. Most people left. They offered coffee and then retreated to the kitchen, because the sound of tuning is not music. It is the same note, over and over, bending slowly toward itself. But he sat on the arm of the sofa and watched.

"How do you know," he said after a while, "when it's right?"

She played two strings of the same note together and held up a finger. "Listen. Hear that wobble? Wah-wah-wah?"

He tilted his head. "Yes."

"That's called a beat. When two strings are almost the same pitch but not quite, they interfere with each other. The closer they get, the slower the beat." She turned the pin a hair's width. The wobble slowed, slowed, and vanished into a single clean tone. "When it's gone, they agree."

"So you just get rid of all the beats."

"No," she said. "That's the strange part."

She had explained this to very few people, because very few people asked, and because it sounded, when said aloud, like a small heartbreak built into the physics of the world.

"If you tune a piano perfectly, every interval pure, with no beats at all, it only sounds right in one key. You could play in C and it would be gorgeous. But move to F-sharp and it's a disaster. The math doesn't close. You go around the circle of fifths and you come back to where you started and you're not where you started. You're a little off."

"So what do you do?"

"You make every interval a little bit wrong. Evenly. On purpose. Every fifth slightly narrow, every third slightly wide. So that nothing is perfect, but everything is usable. You can play in any key." She played a chord, and even on the half-tuned instrument he could hear it, a faint shimmer inside the harmony. "Those beats stay. That's what it costs to be at home everywhere."

Mr. Adair was quiet for a long time. Ines went back to work. The afternoon light moved across the carpet. She tuned through the middle octaves, then the treble, where the strings are short and stubborn and the notes ring like struck glass.

When she reached the high E, she paused. The key stuck slightly, came up slowly, and there was a small nick in the ivory, a sliver missing from the front edge.

"That one's always been like that," said Mr. Adair. He had come to stand behind her. "She dropped a glass on it. Nineteen seventy-something. Wine glass. She was playing and gesturing at the same time, telling me some story, and she knocked it right off the top." He almost smiled. "She said the key never forgave her. Every time she hit it she'd say *sorry, sorry.* Out loud. Forty years."

Ines touched the chipped edge. "I can replace the key top. And fix the sticking. It'd take another visit."

"No," he said, quickly. Then, more slowly: "No. Leave that one."

She nodded. She tuned the string and left the key alone.

It was almost five when she finished. She played a scale up the full length of the keyboard, then a few chords, then, because it seemed the piano deserved it, the first page of a Chopin nocturne she had memorized at fourteen and never forgotten. The instrument woke up under her hands. It had a warm, slightly veiled tone, the sound of old felt and good spruce. Somebody had chosen it carefully once.

When she stopped, Mr. Adair was sitting on the bench beside her. She had not noticed him sit.

"Why did you call me?" she asked. "If nobody plays."

He looked at the keys. "I don't know. I kept walking past it. It felt like leaving someone on hold." He lifted one hand, hesitated, and pressed the high E. It came up slow. The note rang clean and bright into the room.

"Sorry," he said softly, and she understood that he was not speaking to her.

She packed her tools. At the door he paid her in cash, counted twice, and asked whether pianos needed tuning even if they weren't played.

"Twice a year," she said. "The wood moves with the seasons. It drifts."

"Then come back in the spring."

Driving home, she thought about the beats she had left in his piano, hundreds of them, tiny deliberate imperfections tucked inside every chord, so small that most people would never hear them. The price of being able to go anywhere. The shimmer that proves two notes are trying to agree and cannot quite, and are beautiful anyway.

She thought she might tell him about it in the spring. Or she might not. Some things you only understand by sitting next to them for a while, and listening.

I'm considering a few ideas for a short piece—something about a woman who repairs pianos and learns families through their instruments, or an essay on the word "almost"—but I'm settling on a piano tuner story, since tuning offers a nice metaphor to build around.

There's something appealing about equal temperament: every interval is slightly wrong so all keys become playable, meaning true harmony at home requires being a little out of tune everywhere. I'm sketching a plot around this—a tuner named Ines visits an old widower, Mr. Adair, whose untouched piano he still wants tuned, and the story turns on whether she leaves one note imperfect, the one his late wife always got wrong.
